title: Builder.io's /visual-edit skill turns local code into a Figma-like canvas
author: Steve (Builder.io)
essence: Steve (Builder.io) announces /visual-edit, an open-source skill that opens a running local app as URL-backed iframe screens on a Figma-style canvas so agents and humans can make visual edits. The self-thread then hands over the source (github.com/BuilderIO/skills), points to Agent-Native Design, gives the install command (npx @agent-native/core@latest skills add visual-edit) and answers how edits travel: the agent gets a prompt back containing a diff plus metadata such as each element's origin line of code. The captured replies are few but substantive and map straight onto that thread - Logan asks whether an edit 'lands as a diff or as a prompt back to the agent' (the thread answers: a prompt carrying a diff), while Abdul Wasey raises the real design-system risk: 'Dragging 1 card shouldn't quietly change all 20 screens.' One of the three captured replies is an unrelated ad. Sentiment: genuine curiosity with an unresolved component-scoping caveat. 27 replies, 799 likes, 1,082 bookmarks, 45.8K views.
summary: Reusable agent skills are becoming the distribution unit for dev tooling - a free OSS skill is how Builder.io puts its Design surface inside every coding agent.

title: Claude Code skill reverse-engineers any video into a remake recipe
author: Pratzyy
essence: Pratzyy's Claude Code skill /dissect takes any video apart and writes a recipe for remaking its format, demoed left-vs-right on a Kurzgesagt short. The self-thread expands the pitch: it breaks down picture (every cut, shot, caption style, transition), words (transcript, hook, story beats), voice (pace, pauses, pitch), sound (music, SFX, loudness) and audience (most-replayed moments, top comments), accepts YouTube/X/Instagram/TikTok links, and emits one blueprint .md anyone or any AI can follow; install is '/plugin marketplace add 0xpratzyy/dissect' and it is free/open source. The one substantive captured reply sets the quality bar - Thomas M.: 'I like the idea, but you have to say that we're not there yet. Kurzgesagt's one is way better. Intentional, concise... That 10%-5% is what elevates everything' - and Pratzyy concedes in-thread that it is currently a one-shot that improves with more detailed Opus prompts, adding 'this is the worst it will ever be'. A second reply is an unrelated conference ad. 26 replies, 231 likes, 322 bookmarks, 19.4K views.
summary: Reverse-engineering media into a reusable 'recipe' as an agent skill - a template for format-cloning and content-repurposing workflows.

title: Claude Code now supports mods: TypeScript plugins installed via /plugin
author: ClaudeDevs
essence: ClaudeDevs announces that Claude Code can now be modded - change how it behaves, customize the UI, swap in your own features - written in a few lines of TypeScript or generated by Claude, with mods shipping inside plugins and installed via /plugin in the CLI or desktop app. No replies were captured for this post (451 exist), so the substance comes from the six-tweet self-thread: Token Weather forecasts your context window with a sparkline of your last 12 turns; Blast Radius catches risky shell commands like rm -rf, git reset --hard or a force push before they run and shows what they would touch; Replay Theater records every file edit and lets you step through the diffs with /replay. The thread also warns that mods run with the same access to your machine as Claude Code, so only install trusted sources, links claude.ai/directory, offers pre-built sample mods in the Claude Code Playground repo, and notes the team already used mods to build /diff and AGENTS.md support. Biggest post in this slice: 451 replies, 1,375 reposts, 15,763 likes, 10,205 bookmarks, 2.4M views.
summary: Claude Code's plugin/mod layer is a platform moment: whoever ships the winning mods owns a distribution channel inside the agent itself.

title: ChatGPT can now build and deploy MCP servers on ChatGPT Sites
author: Tibo
essence: Tibo (OpenAI) quote-tweets Max Stoiber's launch to say you can now build and deploy MCP servers right through ChatGPT, then restrict their access to anyone you want or share them with the world; the quoted demo runs on '@sites create a todo list', which creates the MCP server, deploys it to Sites and turns it into a plugin. The quoted thread also carries Dishwasher's developer question about whether OpenAI-hosted infrastructure will eventually run backends for plugin extensions, since running a backend is the hard part. Captured replies turn skeptical: TEAGÁ 'nobody cares about Sites and Maps', Tucker King 'Hope people actually use the restrict button', and dearlordylord reporting a live approval bottleneck - his SRD 5e Oracle MCP 'is in approval loop for a month now' (a fourth captured reply is a spam ad). So the debate is about gating and distribution, not the tech. 414 replies, 4,990 likes, 2,156 bookmarks, 768.8K views.
summary: MCP servers become one-click hosted products inside ChatGPT - distribution for MCP builders just got much bigger; watch the hosting, permissions and backend story.

title: OpenClaw cut 400k LOC of tests with a test-audit skill, coverage intact
author: Peter Steinberger 🦞
essence: Peter Steinberger reports that OpenClaw deleted around 400k LOC of its own tests with almost no change in code coverage, crediting a test-audit skill (linked card: openclaw/.agents/skills/test-audit/SKILL.md). His diagnosis: modern models love writing tests for every tiny change even when those tests aren't useful. The self-thread adds the actual technique - 'If you just tell the agent to clean up, it will stop far too early. Give it an ambitious goal', e.g. 'remove 20% of the least useful tests while maintaining code coverage within 2%' - and five days later he notes 'That /goal is still running.' David Cramer's reply extends the argument: models 'also love rewriting tests when they change code as if the reason for those tests in the first place wasnt to prevent regressions'. Sentiment is broad agreement about AI test bloat. 230 replies, 6,699 likes, 10,791 bookmarks, 1.3M views.
summary: Sharpest AI-quality insight in the set: agent-written tests inflate coverage without value, and an audit skill is a cheap way to claw the bloat back.

title: Movie archive spreadsheet: 1300+ films, 800 Blu-ray remuxes, links never expire
author: vilibazmio
essence: vilibazmio's updated public spreadsheet (card: docs.google.com / vilibazmio_archive.xlsx) claims 1,300+ archived movies, nearly 800 Blu-ray remuxes and links that 'will never expire'. The self-thread pre-empts two criticisms: uploads have been live over a year and 'films that aren't mainstream almost never get copyrighted', plus a clarification that the archive 'isn't meant to be used as a streaming platform' - download before watching, and the preview video it sometimes generates is lower quality. Replies split between gratitude and legal unease: snvy asks 'what is the copyright status of these movies?' and warns that enough copyright-holder demands could force archive.org to lock the uploader's account, while Sarvar reports a broken entry ('The Pear Tree (1998) by Dariush Mehrjui... is just an image of the film'). Engagement dwarfs the debate: 114,149 likes, 155,945 bookmarks, 10,079 reposts, 2.8M views, 166 replies.
summary: One evergreen spreadsheet outperformed almost everything in this set - durable, save-worthy link assets work; note the obvious copyright risk before emulating it.

title: One prompt, 8 hours: Claude Code generated an entire app launch video
author: Leon Lin
essence: Leon Lin gave Claude Code (Opus 5.5) one prompt to make a launch video for a fake calendar app and claims everything you see and hear - name, logo, UI, animations, soundtrack, sound effects - is code, after it 'cooked for about 8h'. The self-thread drops the repo (github.com/Leonxlnx/claude-launchvideo) with code, soundtrack and video in it, clarifies the 8h includes reviews and recording (the cloud agent took 30 min), and the author concedes the criticism himself: 'the soundeffects and bg soundtrack don't really match this type of video'. Replies agree on visuals but not audio: mehdi calls it 'by far the best launch video generated by opus 5.5 by a mile', Witti says it is 'master-class' yet dislikes the AI-made music in these videos, and Arthur jokes 'at this point i don't even know if people are joking or not'. 86 replies, 1,279 likes, 1,315 bookmarks, 90.1K views.
summary: End-to-end launch-video production from one prompt is now a working demo - worth planning agent-generated video into your own launch pipeline.

title: Never use staccato sentences in landing pages — design prompt of the day
author: Michael
essence: Michael (@michael_chomsky) design prompt of the day: LLMs write staccato sentences ('More reliable. Less expensive.' / 'Sleep better. Live longer.') — tell your agent to never use staccato sentences in landing pages (OP misspells it 'stacatto' and admits he checked the spelling and still got it wrong; correct spelling is staccato). summary: Copy-paste prompt rule for landing pages, plus two steals: also ban 'it's not X, it's Y' and give the agent a liked-paragraph example instead of pure bans.

title: Leviathan: open-source indexer lets agents search 1M records in ~436 tokens
author: joshua
essence: joshua (@joshuagunnn) open-sources Leviathan (github.com/elstongun/leviathan): one Rust binary so agents search any-size databases without reading them — point at JSONL, CSV or SQLite, or pipe Postgres, MySQL, DuckDB or Mongo; it infers the schema, builds a full-text index and returns short cited cards at ~450 tokens whether 10K or 1M rows. Self-thread: agents reason over five records but drown in a million (grep, paging APIs, dumping whole history into context); at 1M rows 99% of questions get a relevant record in the top 5 with 33ms median, worst case 602 tokens versus grep's 9.7M; under ~100K rows grep is honestly fine. CLI first, MCP optional, because MCP schemas tax every session while a skill file costs zero tokens until called; works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor. Replies: skeptic snow flags it as just FTS5/BM25, nothing new (fair prior-art caution); mbrochh asks for folder and docs indexing beyond DBs; badguyty asks about NoSQL and log streams; OP floats a $10/month hosted auto-index version. 72 replies, 179 reposts, 2.5K likes, 3.7K bookmarks.
summary: Save for agent-plus-large-data work; the token math (436 vs 107K) and CLI-first-over-MCP rule are the keepers — verify BM25/FTS limits before adopting.

title: Devin Dreaming plus Agent Memory Repo: Git-versioned memory graph as OSS standard
author: Cognition
essence: Cognition (@cognition) introduces Dreaming: across sessions Devin builds a memory graph of how you work, and at night it self-improves that memory to remove stale records and discover latent information; alongside it they are creating an OSS standard, Agent Memory Repo (cognition.com/agent-memory-repo; explainer at devin.ai/blog/memory-and-dreaming). Replies: Jared Zoneraich and Chris Wozniczek say they can retire their git-brain and studio-brain repos, with Chris running parallel Devins on interconnected Linear tasks and calling the coordination a massive unlock; Corey Ward hopes it fixes PR reviews flagging non-issues; band.eth asks whether it hallucinates context from old logs (open risk); Elara calls the OSS standard a huge move. 126 replies, 331 reposts, 2.3K likes, 2.2K bookmarks with a video.
summary: Watch the OSS Agent Memory Repo spec — Git-versioned memory files as a cross-session message board is the pattern to copy even outside Devin.

title: Every vibe coder's SEO prompt is actually the whole checklist — paste into Claude Code
author: Suraj Sharma

Make no mistakes.' after SSR, sitemap, Search Console, robots, noindex, redirects, 404s, canonicals, meta descriptions, one H1, FAQ schema, breadcrumbs, orphans, alt text, WebP, CLS, sub-2s loads, de-slop, author bio, backlinks) is actually the whole checklist — bookmark it, paste into Claude Code, and do the last two (bio, backlinks) yourself. title: Deleted 800K lines of unit tests from the monorepo: 3 hypotheses on why tests hurt agents
author: Sherwood
essence: Sherwood (@shcallaway) deleted 800K lines of unit tests from the sazabi monorepo with three hypotheses: tests lock in slop by making code hard to change, slow dev cycles via extra agent work and CI time, and waste money via agent tokens and useless CI runs — results to follow. Replies split: Stefano cries AI psychosis; Kevin gives the key counter (good tests assert behavior, not implementation); kamera answers with sarcasm (next delete the build configs); Andrew dares them to push to prod. 377 replies, 248 reposts, 3.3K likes, 2.1K bookmarks, 621K views.
summary: The strongest anti-unit-test datapoint for agent workflows — pair it with Kevin's behavior-not-implementation counter before acting.

title: Claude Code's 'You should Know' plugin: a sideagent that catches what you missed
author: ClaudeDevs

Replies: Behnam finds the demos confusing and asks for plain-English mod explanations in ASD-STE100 (see X-278); David calls it the worst feature since every turn ends in more work, suggesting piping output back to resolve; Lucas asks about verbosity control; Chris asks about Cloud sessions; Adam asks about subscription cost; Neil jokes about paying to condense word salad. 378 replies, 1155 reposts, 16K likes, 16.8K bookmarks, 1.6M views.

title: Opus 5.5 sound pass: prompt that measures beats and mixes to -16 LUFS
author: Vox
essence: Vox shares a copy-paste sound pass for Opus 5.5 motion videos so they stop sounding like cheap electronic beeps: tell the model it cannot hear so it must measure every step (install ffmpeg + librosa first); use licensed music only (a supplied track or Mixkit free license, with source noted, never synthesized); find beats with librosa but verify against a sub-120Hz waveform plot and shift the grid if kicks misalign (he caught a 0.22s off-beat this way); land cuts and title moves on beats (edit the animation or move the music start); attach one ready-made SFX per move (whoosh/pop/click/typing, prefer the project library like HyperFrames); keep voiceover loudest with music ducked, targeting -16 LUFS with peaks below -4 dBFS measured on the exported MP4 via ffmpeg ebur128 (not the WAV) so it survives AAC and phone-mono playback; then grab pre/post frames per cue, plot waveforms, and return 5 timestamps for headphone checks without claiming it sounds good. Replies praise the LUFS/phone detail, call the prompt a QA pipeline disguised as a brief, and plug @audioascode; 14 replies, 579 likes, 973 bookmarks.
summary: A reusable audio post-production prompt for AI motion video - the librosa off-beat check and MP4-only loudness measurement are the save-worthy bits.

title: Run LinkedIn ads on every potential investor for a month before raising
author: Harsha from Slashy
essence: Harsha's underrated fundraising alpha: before raising, run LinkedIn ads against every single potential investor for one month (about 5k spend) to manufacture familiarity and FOMO. His follow-up adds they got VC inbound accidentally the same way through paid email clients, noting a good chunk of paid-email users are VCs. Replies split: a top quote-tweet calls it the top of dumb ideas, one says 'Delete this' (keep the alpha secret), others ask about conversion proof, whether it is illegal (tagged to Grok), and joke it only works if investors are in high school; 23 replies, 1,085 likes, 1,255 bookmarks, 264K views.
summary: A cheap pre-raise familiarity play - worth testing with a tight investor list and reply-rate tracking rather than assuming FOMO.

title: Lintapple: tell your agent to install it so AI stops making bad UI
author: Gavin
essence: Gavin claims it should be impossible for AI to make a bad UI and ships lintapple: tell your agent to install and set it up in the project (github.com/gholtzap/lintapple), demo on video. Replies roast the corner radius ('what the fuck is that corner radius' - author asks what it should be instead), a paper-UI user shows interest, one will try it with the author promising to keep coding until it is useful for everyone; one reply is an unrelated WhatsApp-SDK ad. 25 replies, 1,227 likes, 2,506 bookmarks.

title: DigUp: on-device semantic file search for Mac with EmbeddingGemma 2
author: Abdur Rahim

Replies propose combining the index approach with FSearch, which the author will look at; the rest are ads. 15 replies, 406 likes, 516 bookmarks.

author: Hassan

Replies show convergent evolution - cultist_dev built the same thing (Jeff, a bookshelf you can ask), thekitze praises the visual beauty, the author reacts to heavy readers; one reply is a product ad. 98 replies, 2,659 likes, 2,406 bookmarks.

author: Florence

title: ManimGX: 90x-faster 3D animation engine built for agents
author: Sina Atalay
essence: Sina introduces ManimGX, an open-source 3D animation engine built for agents: 90x faster than ManimCE (36s of 1080p60 in 3.1s; 11.5x ManimGL, 18.7x Blender Workbench, method in the repo benchmarks), Rust + wgpu core, compatible with Manim's Python API, one pip install with no system dependencies (no LaTeX/FFmpeg, 65-110MB), and it even runs in the browser via Pyodide and WebGPU. Agent-native touches: a manimgx inspect CLI that storyboards PNGs for the agent to check before rendering, 2D layout checks (cutoff, overlap, size), fully statically typed APIs, and an llms.txt try-it prompt. 66 replies, 2,610 likes, 4,184 bookmarks.
summary: The speed plus llms.txt plus inspect-loop combo is the template for making any renderer agent-operable.

title: Anatomy: one line in, interactive 3D machine out, as a Claude skill
author: R
essence: R introduces Anatomy: describe a machine in one line and Claude brings it to life - interactive isometric wireframes to rotate and inspect, WebGL shaders for fire/water/plasma, real 3D motion with individually moving parts; installable as an agent skill, fully open source (github.com/wheresryan22/anatomy). title: Run GitHub Actions locally with act instead of push-wait loops
author: Divy
essence: Replying to Branko's complaint about testing GitHub Actions through commit-push-wait-4-minutes loops, Divy recommends nektos/act for running Actions locally (linked repo card). Branko knows it and says local runs just feel better; a follow-up pitches preloop as the agent-native alternative, noting act does not implement the official protocol (divergences happen) and runs containers rather than microVMs. 3 replies, 63 likes, 126 bookmarks.

title: Cloudflare security-audit skill found real vulns via 26 Codex agents
author: Elif
essence: Elif recommends Cloudflare's security-audit-skill (github.com/cloudflare/security-audit-skill): she gave it to Codex, 26 agents found real vulnerabilities - non-obvious ones her own months-long tests missed. title: Raise subagent prompt-cache TTL to 1h for long-running Claude subagents
author: alex getman

Replies push back hard: leeovery calls it awful blind advice since a 1h cache costs more for 2-minute subagents, the author concedes it depends on workload (5+ minute gaps between calls expire the cache), CesarMilagent says ask Claude first, and mooroobee notes 5 minutes is between turns so an active subagent is normally fine. 90 replies, 1,637 likes, 2,991 bookmarks.
summary: A one-line cost/latency lever for subagent-heavy setups - but read the counterarguments before applying it blindly.

title: InstaBox prices agent cloud around a free 4 vCPU machine and cheap unit economics
author: Hang Huang
essence: Day 1 of InstaBox's 28-day 'test in prod' series is the pricing page: one free 4 vCPU / 8 GB machine with no usage limit, plus what Hang Huang calls the most competitive unit price on the market. He credits oversubscription and high utilization for the low cost, and explicitly copies Cloudflare's two principles - free users do QA and force a more intuitive product. 1,000 more invite codes go out; early users keep five free machines until Dec 1, and a Grok bot picks commenters to DM. The 123 replies are almost entirely invite-code begging and use-case pitches (Godot games, agent hosting), with little pricing scrutiny.
summary: A candid look at pricing dev infra around a generous free tier and utilization economics - useful as a pricing-strategy read, not as independent proof of the 'best unit price' claim.

title: A free Opus 5.5 SEO assistant that audits and rewrites your site every week
author: Theo
essence: Theo built an SEO assistant on Opus 5.5 that takes a website, finds and applies fixes, identifies real competitors, tracks keywords and rankings, and produces a prioritized weekly action plan. title: Indra OCR 1.1: 1M-param model does 44 pages/s on CPU and adds 80+ languages
author: Vik Paruchuri
essence: Datalab's 1.1 update keeps the 1M-parameter main OCR model and claims 44 pages/s on CPU, within four points of the 3.4B-parameter DeepSeek OCR 2 on OmniParseBench, 15x faster than Tesseract, and support for 80+ languages plus limited handwriting. title: The SaaS directory playbook: seven high-authority listings that feed AI discovery
author: Taras
essence: Taras spent a week publishing a chain of seven 'visibility hack' posts, each quoting the previous one: Zapier (REST integration, ~3-day approval), the Official MCP Registry (DNS TXT ownership proof, no review queue, and the list hundreds of directories and clients pull from), the Claude Community directory (needs a two-seat Teams plan at $40/mo and is noindex), Vercel Connectors, Glama (auto-imports registry entries, grades tool descriptions, health-checks listings), Smithery (27,000+ servers, gateway trials, dofollow link) and ClawHub (OpenClaw's skill registry, security-audited, dofollow). Replies report Zapier approving in three days, a 403 on Smithery submissions, and skepticism about DR-chasing; Taras says the Claude directory drives the most usage but is only for visibility, while the real win is entity/brand presence across sources AI already trusts.
summary: One consolidated playbook instead of seven near-identical posts: publish a real MCP server, land the Official Registry first, then cascade to the directories that matter and skip the noindex ones.

title: Agent tree component shows which agent spawned which
author: Flo
essence: Design engineer Flo demos an agent-tree UI component that visualizes parent/child agent relationships - who started whom. The 2.7K-like reaction is mostly design admiration for his component library, with practical questions about the stack (BaseUI, shadcn, Radix), whether a parent's cost includes its children, and requests to port it to Claude Desktop, t3 code and Supacode. Suggested improvements: keep the parent sticky while scrolling long child lists, and show children that outlive a stopped parent. No code or link is included.

title: Treg AEO toolkit shows which sources AI cites and who wrote them
author: Treg
essence: Treg launched an open-source AEO toolkit that finds every source an AI cites and the author behind it, then helps get your product into those sources - priced at 1 cent per prompt with no subscription and access to 4,000+ data/services. The repo is superdesigndev/treg, with CloroAI as partner. Replies treat the pricing as the story: 1 cent to 'win a prompt' in ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini versus $50/month minimums elsewhere, and several users say Treg is already part of their SEO workflow. One describes it as an 'AEO agent' rather than another dashboard.
summary: A cheap, open-source way to inspect and influence the citations AI models actually use - more actionable than most AEO dashboards.

title: agent-browser snapshot --delta cuts form-filling tokens by 73x
author: Chris Tate
essence: Vercel Labs' agent-browser added 'snapshot --delta', which returns only what changed since the previous snapshot instead of the whole page; the demo shows 73x fewer tokens while filling a form. The thread clarifies that delta state resets between sessions, so for long gaps you should save a baseline and run 'agent-browser diff snapshot --baseline last.txt'. Replies are enthusiastic (Rauch: 'Epic'), but the useful pushback is that 73x is a best-case minimal form, an empty delta is ambiguous between unchanged and never-loaded, and '--full' is worth re-sending after context compaction.
summary: A concrete token-cost win for repeated agent/browser loops - use a saved baseline for long-running monitors and treat empty deltas with suspicion.

title: Skill-issue.in is a ranked directory for AI agent skills
author: Palak
essence: Palak posts a bare link to Skill-issue.in, which surfaces and ranks agent skills. The 4K-like, 9.2K-bookmark reaction is out of proportion to the one-line post, and replies supply the context: it overlaps with skills.sh and the wave of skill directories, the site's own design could use the skills it ranks, and the ranking mechanic is the differentiator. Several people ask what it is or which skill is most useful; nobody posts a rigorous comparison.

title: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash is free in OpenCode; Kuvo Code runs bot teams on it
author: serhat
essence: Serhat points out that DeepSeek V4.1 Flash is free on OpenCode right now, so you can run a whole team of bots in Kuvo Code at zero cost. Kuvo's bots now hold standups: a lead splits the work and each bot executes its part. He clarifies that Kuvo uses the OpenCode engine, works offline, and does not require an OpenCode account; the recent OpenCode breach affected only Console users. Replies are wary - the breach, aggressive rate limits, model-switch crashes, and questions about Windows/mobile support dominate.
summary: A free way to experiment with multi-agent 'standup' workflows, with the honest caveat that free-model rate limits and OpenCode's breach are real risks.

title: One command gives coding agents persistent memory via supermemory
author: supermemory
essence: Supermemory's pitch is a single command - npx supermemory plugins - that adds persistent memory to coding agents, with a console for management. Replies surface the practical issues: copy-pasting the stylized Unicode command from the tweet fails, people want to know if it is open source and how it compares to Hindsight, and one user argues stale memories should decay rather than be related to new ones because they cause drift. The positive replies focus on how hard memory is and how much a one-liner helps.
summary: A low-friction memory layer worth testing, but the command must be retyped (not copied from the styled text) and memory-decay policy is still an open design question.

title: REA babysitting prompt turns free GLM-5.3-Flash into a reverse-engineering analyst
author: qwerty__cs
essence: The 'REA Reverse Engineering Babysitting Tutorial' is a four-step workflow: install OpenCode, pick the free GLM-5.3-Flash model, paste the prompt shown in the image, and let the agent drive REA (Reverse Engineer Anything). The prompt is a structured operating contract - objective, requirements, decisions, work state - demanding evidence anchors (path/line/address/md5), four-part reports, and strict rules about worktrees, file writes and uploads. Replies are split: a reverse engineer with IDA experience calls it overhyped versus IDA MCP + AI, while others confirm Frida memory hooks work until Zhipu patches the free window. The best tips are to split decompilation into a module inventory then per-module deep dives (context truncation), and to expect queue variability on the free tier.
summary: A reusable prompt structure for agent-assisted RE, not a magic button - treat the 'no bans' claim skeptically and verify findings against real tooling.

title: Buy yourbrandreviews.com so LLMs quote reviews you control
author: james
essence: James suggests buying two domains - yourapp.com and yourappreviews.com - and hosting your own reviews there, so when users ask an LLM for reviews it pulls from a page you control. He calls it a dirty little secret everyone will do within 24 months. Replies are hostile and specific: no evidence is offered, the FTC's 2024 fake-review rule bans company-controlled sites posing as independent reviews (roughly $50k per violation), a new low-authority domain will not outrank Trustpilot/G2, and models can be updated to distrust it. He insists he never suggested fake reviews, only hosting real ones.
summary: A legally and ethically risky growth hack with no evidence behind it - worth knowing as a dark pattern, not worth copying.

title: Garry Tan pairs Capy and Aside so agents code and set up DevOps
author: Garry Tan
essence: Garry Tan's favorite new-project combo is Capy (agents write the first version) plus Aside (agents handle the DevOps), so the first code and the deploy pipeline happen in one flow. Replies are a mix of enthusiasm and warnings: Cloudflare's primitives are simpler in one account, 'devops is where most weekend projects die', one user claims Capy auto-uploads agent trajectories without consent, and others ask whether the agent handles 2FA or re-auth every run. The most useful counterpoint is that agent-owned deploys can create outages nobody understands.
summary: An influential endorsement of end-to-end agent building - useful as a workflow pointer, but read the privacy and operability warnings in the replies.

title: Weespy Chrome extension reverse-spies a SaaS's traffic, ads and content
author: Mathias Chapelon
essence: Mathias Chapelon launches Weespy, a free Chrome extension that shows how any SaaS gets customers: traffic estimates, tech stack, ads, SEO, and what competitors post on X, LinkedIn and Reddit, in one click. The thread walks through installing it, listing competitors, and copying formats that already perform. Replies ask whether traffic estimates come from SimilarWeb, whether it shows abandoned channels, and whether it can tailor social content to an audience - most go unanswered. The launch video itself was made with Opus 5.5 + Remotion.
summary: A free, fast competitor-research starting point - just treat traffic numbers as estimates and verify anything before betting a strategy on it.

title: Amazon blocks AI shopping agents; Maritime's Android MCP stays logged in for $1/month
author: Maritime (YC F26)
essence: Amazon blocked AI assistants such as Muse, Dots and Instinct from browsing and buying on its site. Maritime pitches a workaround: its Android MCP spins up a persistent Android phone in the cloud, shops on Amazon for the customer, and stays logged in for next time - for $1/month per agent. Replies are sparse; Hunch says it can still use Amazon through a direct connector. The post is a small but clear signal that commerce platforms are starting to fight agent traffic, and infrastructure layers are routing around it.
summary: A useful data point on the coming agent-vs-commerce-platform access fight - and a reminder that 'persistent logged-in phone' workarounds carry account and ToS risk.

title: Object storage benchmark: Railway/Tigris fastest, Neon slowest and priciest
author: Leo
essence: Leo benchmarked S3, Cloudflare R2, Railway Buckets, Backblaze B2 and Neon Object Storage from six locations using the Files SDK for fairness. Railway was fastest on time-to-first-byte and 100 MB downloads from every location; R2 was fastest for 1 MB uploads overall but slowest from Virginia; Railway was also cheapest, while S3 and Neon were expensive. The benchmark code and site are open source. Replies congratulate Neon on being both slowest and most expensive, note that Railway's S3 is Tigris under the hood, and ask for Tigris itself to be tested.
summary: Rare public, reproducible storage numbers - Railway/Tigris look like the value pick, but rerun the benchmark for your own regions and file sizes.

title: The AGENTS.md 'two-way doors' rule that doubled one dev's shipping
author: Dara A.
essence: Dara's AGENTS.md section tells agents: walk through two-way doors and show me after; stop at one-way doors. If the answer would be a rubber stamp, don't ask; if running something can answer the question, run it. Save questions for taste and product calls only, one at a time, with a recommendation, and 'no' is acceptable. Once a one-way door is opened it stays open for that work, including subagents, and the agent should return only if the door turns out different (more at stake, a check failing, something unknown). Replies focus on how much decision fatigue this removes and debate whether harnesses can be trusted with that autonomy.
summary: A compact, copy-pasteable autonomy contract that trades permission-seeking for stated reversibility - the best AGENTS.md snippet in this batch.

title: Send Opus 5.5 three test accounts and 14 real attacks before shipping
author: Vox
essence: Vox turns a vibe-coded app's pre-launch security review into a concrete red-team script: three subagents with three accounts (A, B, admin) run 14 attacks across impersonation, limit bypass and outside access, collect proof, then fix everything in one pass. The attacks are specific - query every table with the public key, swap A's id for B's, inject role: admin into a profile update, reuse a password-reset link, call APIs past the UI and credit limits, test open redirects with // and @, XSS in usernames and Markdown, SSRF against localhost and 169.254.169.254, cache leakage between accounts, unauthenticated preview links, and prompt injection through uploaded documents. Every item must actually run, and a fix only counts if the attack succeeds with protection off and fails with it on. The replies are a warning label: several users say this pattern gets Claude accounts flagged or downgraded, and recommend local models instead.
summary: A reusable, unusually concrete security checklist for agent-built apps - but run it against your own test environment, not a production account you care about.

title: Reloop undercuts Resend at $20 per 100K emails and adds inbound mail
author: Pranav Patel
essence: Pranav Patel launches Reloop, an open-source email platform positioned as a cheaper Resend: 100K emails for $20/month instead of $90, free to 3,000, with an email API, SMTP relay, inboxes for AI agents, automations, deliverability guardrails, bring-your-own-SMTP and inbound email. It is agentic (the whole UI is available to an AI) and self-hostable. The 'I reverse engineered Resend' framing is what the thread fights about: the top reply says vibe-coding a clone is not reverse engineering and that open-source Resend alternatives have existed for years, another says the price matches Resend without its reliability, and others ask how much was him versus a model. Patel answers that the architecture and decisions are his, that Reloop is not an AWS wrapper, and links a PR adding it to the opencoredev email SDK.
summary: A credible cheap Resend alternative if deliverability holds up - the launch is also a case study in how 'reverse engineered' framing invites credit and reliability scrutiny.

title: Earshot gives coding agents ears to judge and generate sound effects
author: Leon Lin
essence: Leon Lin's earshot is an MCP server and skill that lets a coding agent describe, match and find sound effects, render a visual page of a soundtrack, and critique audio with scores plus timestamped fixes - all locally on CPU. Earshot Forge goes further: the agent writes code to synthesize a sound, listens to it, scores it, rewrites the code and repeats until it is decent, comparing against real recordings because blind tests mislead. Lin's own blind test of 15 real-vs-generated pairs got 8 right, essentially a coin flip, which he admits. Setup is one command: claude mcp add earshot -- python -m earshot mcp. The launch video's entire soundtrack was made in code, but the top replies are blunt that it still sounds like sloppy Claude sound design, which is the problem the tool is meant to fix.
summary: A genuinely new modality for coding agents - audio QA and synthesis in one loop - though the demos show taste is still the bottleneck, not generation.

title: OpenDesign Motion makes agent videos with any model, no Opus required
author: OpenDesign
essence: OpenDesign Motion is an open-source alternative to Claude Motion that decouples motion-video generation from one model: any agent and any model can drive it, and the launch video itself was made in OpenDesign. The thread is a demo reel for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, showing tutorial-style motion graphics, a self-made launch video and multiple demos made without Opus 5.5. The author says it renders locally and new users get free trial credits. Replies split between people wanting to try it and motion designers unimpressed by the output - 'fast cuts with colourful distractions' that ignore motion-graphics principles - which is the same taste gap that shows up in every code-generated video launch.
summary: The interesting claim is model independence and local rendering, not the demo quality; treat it as an option to test against Claude Motion rather than a drop-in upgrade.

title: Sys0 launches an interactive systems course and gets accused of repackaging open source
author: Rakesh K
essence: Rakesh K launched sys0.in, an interactive way to learn systems programming, and the reply section turned into a plagiarism trial. Multiple replies accuse him of taking the open-source breakscale.tech, adding a paywall and charging around ₹4,000; one calls it '1:1 cloning' and another says big creators are copying college students' open-source work. Rakesh denies it and tells critics to try the free lessons and lab before concluding, while defenders say the step-by-step labs are original and the free tier is real. The launch itself is thin - a link and 'try interacting with it' - so the durable signal is the accusation pattern, not the product detail.
summary: A launch buried by a copying scandal: useful as a reminder to document provenance and licensing before monetizing an educational product, whatever the truth here.

title: DreamScale runs frontier robot models from a one-line prompt, no GPU
author: Chris Yoo
essence: DreamScale Labs launched a hosted way to run physical-AI models on robots through a single sentence - 'I want to run a <model> on a <robot> to <do something>' - with no GPU and real-time inference over the cloud. It starts with MolmoAct2, pi0.5 and Flux 3 Action, and the simulator runs in the browser while making cloud inference calls. The pitch is that model/robot/task combinations are too confusing to evaluate, so the UI collapses them into one prompt. Replies immediately hit the two hard questions: how do you evaluate model quality across different robots, and whether cloud inference can survive packet loss and latency in safety-critical physical systems. Neither got a concrete answer in the thread.
summary: A clean interface over a genuinely messy problem; the missing evaluation and latency story is what determines whether it is a demo or infrastructure.

title: A Codex-built whey price bot found a 2 kg deal the apps buried
author: Vijay
essence: Vijay asked Codex to reverse engineer an Android quick-commerce price-comparison app, pulled its backend endpoints with the REA skill, and built a whey-protein price-alert bot. It paid off immediately: 2 kg for ₹3,993 on Instamart when the going rate was ₹3,200+ for 1 kg. He says the bot polls twice a day, that proxies are the real operational headache because sites block scrapers, and that the whole thing is easy enough to vibe-code now. Replies ask for the repo, the polling rate and which whey; the more useful skepticism is that reverse-engineering works when the target API is clean but falls apart on messy DOMs, and that IP/account blocking is the part nobody demos.
summary: A small, concrete example of agent-built scraping economics - the win is the endpoint discovery, the hidden cost is proxies and anti-bot maintenance.

title: Epstein.md is a 927K-character markdown file for banning AI design slop
author: Shipper
essence: Shipper released epstein.md, a 927,400+ character markdown file meant to stop vibe-coded UI from looking like AI slop: no box shadows, no emojis, no green 'LIVE' badges, zero blue-purple gradients, and a blocklist of 350 overused AI words (delve, vibe, seamless). It is the product of 11 months of eight-hour doomscrolling and continuous additions to their own vibecoder, and it is integrated into shipper.now. The reaction is split between people who want the file and people dunking on the name and on the launch video, which itself uses checkmark emojis and looks like the slop it claims to ban. Several replies are simply 'what .md?' - the post never links the file directly, which blunts the distribution.
summary: A memorable anti-slop ruleset with a self-inflicted naming and packaging problem; the content may be useful, but the launch is a case study in how a joke name can overshadow the artifact.

title: Bryel offers a domain-specific model trained from one prompt in seven days
author: Kevin Miao
essence: Kevin Miao pitches Bryel Foundry as model training reduced to one prompt: give it a teacher model and a domain, and within seven days you get a custom model up to 2x cheaper in that domain. The proof point is Coinbase's 9B model, which reportedly beat frontier models in its domain while being 55% faster and costing under $100 to train. Bryel says it has used the same tooling to train models for unicorns and is now opening it to outside teams, with a demo booking link. Replies are interested but probe the obvious weak spot - whether a model trained this way holds up on messy, unseen data - and Miao answers that the harder problem is keeping up as real-world inputs evolve, which is why continuous retraining matters.
summary: Model training as a service is getting cheap enough to try; the claim to verify is out-of-distribution robustness, not the headline training cost.

title: TasteSkill v2 gives coding agents art direction, real assets and a browser check
author: Leon Lin
essence: Leon Lin rebuilt TasteSkill from scratch: v2 reads a brief, writes down what is specific to that client, has a script choose three directions from twenty it researched, and then makes the agent gather real photos, maps and other assets with credits before building. A browser check verifies the result instead of trusting the model's self-report. The install is npx skills add Leonxlnx/taste-skill, and the repo includes example credits. Lin is candid that it is 'just some markdown files' and cannot solve general design taste, and the replies bear that out - some call it their go-to skill, others say the showcased outputs still look like AI slop. The launch video was itself coded with Cinetic and Opus 5.5.
summary: The strongest part is the workflow - research, constrained direction choice, real assets, browser verification - not a promise that markdown can replace a designer.

title: Design.how ships a copy-paste design system for AI apps and dev tools
author: Arlan Marat
essence: Arlan Marat published a new design system aimed specifically at AI apps and developer tools, with copyable code at design.how/systems. The post is deliberately minimal - a link and 'new design system' - but the replies show the niche it fills: people are tired of agents 'creatively reinterpreting' a palette into six shades of purple, and a constrained system gives them something concrete to build against. Marat says his own agent came up with it, which is either a useful signal about agent-generated design systems or a warning about how little human curation is behind it, depending on your priors.
summary: A lightweight, copy-paste starting point for AI-product UI; the value is constraint and speed, not originality.

title: A 15-year-old founder's full agent stack: t3, pstack, Notion, Linear and three cloud agents
author: Leo
essence: Leo, a 15-year-old founder shipping viral projects every one to two weeks, documents his whole setup: t3 code to remote into a Mac mini/Linux box, a custom pstack built for t3 and ov2, everything on a home server with Tailscale previews. Opus 5.5 is the daily driver, GPT-6.1 Sol reviews changes and sometimes does backend work, Haiku 5.5 handles codebase search and docs. Notion is long-term memory for both him and the agents, every thread starts as a Linear issue (even tiny fixes) so state is tracked and linked to the PR, and agents must test in a browser. He adds anti-slop oxlint rules, Paper for design, a mix of Capy/Hoplite/Devin for cloud work, Grok bot for managing agents, and Convex when a backend is needed. The most-asked question is for his custom pstack; his answer is to give the post to your agent and have it adapt the setup.
summary: Less a tool list than an operating model: one issue per thread, explicit memory, model specialization and browser-verified changes - copy the structure, not the exact stack.

title: InstaBox launches sub-second cloud computers for AI agents, then publishes the pricing
author: Hang Huang
essence: Hang Huang launched InstaBox, cloud computers for AI agents: a 4 vCPU / 8 GB machine spun up in under a second, built-in computer use, snapshots for cloning, persistent files/packages/config and public URLs for local ports. The launch was invite-only, with early access including 20 vCPU and 40 GB RAM free, and the reply count - 2,732 - is almost entirely people asking for codes or pitching use cases (Godot games, agent hosting, multi-agent chat rooms). Five days later the same account published the pricing rationale: one free 4 vCPU machine with no usage limit, aggressive oversubscription economics and Cloudflare-style free-tier logic. The two posts together are a rare public view of launch demand turning into a pricing decision.
summary: A strong launch signal for agent-native cloud infra; the follow-up pricing post is the more useful artifact because it explains the unit economics behind the free tier.

title: One paste-in prompt had Opus 5.5 find four performance bugs in three hours
author: Emanuele Di Pietro
essence: Emanuele Di Pietro gave Opus 5.5 on Extra High a single performance prompt and let it run for three hours on his app. It found four bugs he had missed: big chats now open 27% faster, switching back is 2x faster, scroll jumps dropped 98%, and reloads fetch the chat once instead of twice; scrolling old messages does 20% less work. The prompt is the artifact - improve startup, screen-open time, content loading and scrolling, find the real bottleneck, apply fixes, and benchmark before and after each one - and the benchmark requirement is what replies single out as the difference between real optimization and cosmetic refactoring. The test app was trysynara.com; one skeptic jokes that the only measurable outcome was a bigger Cloudflare bill.
summary: A compact, reusable performance prompt whose key instruction is per-fix before/after measurement, not the model or the three-hour runtime.

title: Indra launches a 1M-parameter OCR model at 49 pages/s on CPU
author: Vik Paruchuri
essence: Datalab's Indra is a 1M-parameter OCR model built for CPU latency: 49 pages/s, 11x faster than PaddleOCR and 17x faster than Tesseract, with an OmniParseBench text score of 41.3 versus 35.8 and 19.3. It returns full layout and line bounding boxes, covers 60 languages and six scripts (Latin, Cyrillic, Greek, Devanagari, Bengali, Chinese), handles any script present in a PDF text layer, and has a special math mode. The trade-off is explicit: at 1M parameters, handwriting, complex tables and large pages degrade, and Datalab points those cases to Chandra. A pip install plus indra-ocr-viewer gives a local speed/settings tester. Replies ask for Telugu, Arabic and Hebrew, report failures on slightly skewed pages, and one developer has already ported it to WASM and runs it in production.
summary: A purpose-built triage/ingestion OCR model: choose it for throughput on clean documents, and route hard pages to a larger model rather than expecting one tiny model to do everything.

title: Reason claims Codex+Astra-level Terminal-Bench performance at 22% lower cost
author: Reason
essence: Reason launched a coding harness pitched on cost efficiency: it says it beats Codex+Astra on Terminal-Bench 4.0 while costing 22% less, and it offers an unlimited free local tier alongside a Pro product. You can bring your own subscription or API, and the team published its work and a blog explaining the agent. The 678K views and 178 replies made it one of the bigger launches in this batch, but the thread is skeptical rather than celebratory: several users ask how it can be free when the last version demanded money before disappearing, others call it too good to be true, and one asks for a comparison against open-source harnesses. The Terminal-Bench claim is the one to reproduce before trusting the cost claim.
summary: A cost-focused coding harness worth benchmarking yourself; the free tier and the benchmark claim both need independent verification given the team's prior pricing flip-flop.

title: SlashDocs is Google Docs for the HTML and Markdown agents generate
author: Shashank Kumar
essence: Shashank Kumar open-sourced SlashDocs, a collaboration hub for the HTML and Markdown documents agents now generate. It hosts decks, dashboards and reports in one place, with sharing, permissions and inline comments, and agents can read the feedback and update the same document instead of generating another file and another link. The proof is internal scale at Razorpay: 28,000+ documents created, and more than half of all documents generated there now live in SlashDocs. It is self-hosted, agent-agnostic and open source, with a hosted entry point at razorpay.com/slash-docs. Replies probe the obvious gaps - native Slack integration, how agents read comments (MCP?), comparison with Notion - and one reports a scroll bug, which is fair for a freshly open-sourced product.
summary: A sensible missing layer for agent output: one canonical, commentable document instead of a trail of regenerated files and links.

title: Appllama's open-source skills reverse engineer any app, design or interaction
author: jaimin
essence: jaimin points at the Appllama skills repo with a simple pitch - 'any app. any design. any interaction' - framed as the next step beyond a viral reverse-engineering demo: 'you think this is cool? wait until you find out about...' The skills are open-source and free, work with all models, and jaimin recommends Codex because it has native image generation, which helps when the target is a visual interface. The quoted post is just 'Reverse Engineer Anything. Software is done.' Replies ask which model to use and whether Appllama itself is now fully paywalled, which matters because the skills are only useful if the underlying service is still accessible.
summary: A free skill pack for cloning app flows and UI; the repo is the artifact, the 'software is done' framing is marketing.

title: Delete 40K lines of tests, then lint the agent so it cannot write them again
author: Kyle Mistele
essence: Kyle Mistele deleted 40,000 lines of tests, added a pile of oxlint rules to stop the agent from recreating them, and built a control loop that gardens and prunes what remains. The deleted tests were specific anti-patterns, not all tests: anything that mocks modules instead of using Effect's dependency injection and test layers, plus the usual low-value React unit tests. The control loop is documented as a design-control-loop skill on skills.sh, and he says the full thing will be open-sourced. Replies are mostly people asking for the rules, with one useful counterpoint that agents have already stopped writing obviously vacuous tests and the remaining cases are subtler - which is exactly where lint heuristics get hard.
summary: A strong pattern for keeping agent-written test suites from bloating: encode the banned test shapes as lint rules and let a loop prune the rest.

title: Huashu-art-motion gives Opus 5.5 35 coded art styles plus a film QA agent
author: Vox
essence: Vox's huashu-art-motion is a skill that lets Opus 5.5 generate animations in 35 art styles by writing code: 17 that work for any subject (Van Gogh, Seurat, Bauhaus, Ghibli watercolor, 8-bit, vaporwave), 18 for art-history time travel (Monet, Klimt, Dalí, Hopper, cave painting, Greek pottery) and 9 explainer styles (3Blue1Brown, keynote, whiteboard, Vox explainer, Kurzgesagt). Each style specifies what actually moves, music is synthesized note-by-note on a BPM grid, and a QA script plus an independent subagent watches the finished film. The delivery script blocks more than 0.3 seconds of blank frames and blue-purple backgrounds over 30% of the film, which it explicitly labels AI slop. Docs are Chinese; the post includes a long English prompt to drive it.
summary: A unusually complete motion-generation pipeline - style cards, beat-synced audio, independent QA and anti-slop gates - worth trying if you already generate video with code.

title: FSearch 0.2: 150x faster grep on just-edited files and a 74% smaller index
author: Noah
essence: Noah shipped FSearch 0.2, a macOS Finder replacement with a much smaller and faster index: 150x faster to grep a file you just edited, a 74% smaller index (1.5 GB to 388 MB for him), 35% more files covered, 65% less daemon memory on Chromium and 32% less peak memory while indexing. He is explicit that raw speed is not the goal - some areas regress by 0.4x - and that the focus is system impact and coverage, which is why he calls comparisons to fff apples-to-oranges. The repo is public, and the demo videos were made by asking Claude to record them. Replies ask about Homebrew and Windows support, and one makes the sharp point that reading edited files while the index catches up is the feature that actually matters.
summary: A Finder replacement optimized for low system cost and fresh-file search, not benchmark bragging rights; the small index with broader coverage is the interesting trade.

title: Treg open-sources people search for Claude at $0.0089 per lead
author: Treg
essence: Treg released an open-source people-search tool for Claude: $0.0089 per lead instead of $600 subscriptions, number one on People Search Bench, zero markup and fully open source. Setup is deliberately agent-native - paste 'set up treg - https://treg.to/llms.txt' into Claude or Codex - and the repo is the same superdesigndev/treg codebase behind its earlier AEO toolkit. The pitch lands because it unbundles one afternoon of research from a monthly subscription, which is exactly what the top replies say they wanted. Others report good results with Hermes and appreciate that Treg shows the cost of each action before running it, while B2B lead-list questions remain unanswered.
summary: A cheap, open alternative to subscription people-search tools; the per-lead pricing and pre-run cost display are the parts worth copying.

title: Maritime (YC F26) hosts each AI agent on its own computer for $1/month
author: Maria Gorskikh
essence: Maria Gorskikh launched Maritime, a YC F26 company giving startups infrastructure to deploy, manage and scale agents, each with its own computer, starting at $1 per agent per month. The thread keeps the math deliberately simple - 500 agents is $500 - so founders can reason about cost without a spreadsheet. Early users reply that they have already set it up and that it is special, while the sharper questions are about what the bill looks like at real scale and whether the launch video's people were agents or founders. Five days later the same company used the platform to demo a persistent Android phone for shopping on Amazon after Amazon blocked AI assistants, which is a more concrete illustration of the 'each agent gets a computer' thesis than the launch copy.
summary: A clean per-agent pricing model for agent infrastructure; the Amazon Android demo is the proof that persistent, logged-in computers are the actual product.

title: fframes recreates a viral video with Rust, SVG and shaders - and beats the original's polish
author: Dmitriy Kovalenko
essence: Dmitriy Kovalenko answered a 'let's see AI recreate this' challenge by rebuilding the video as an fframes project with Codex, using only Rust, SVG and shaders. He argues the result is better than the original: fframes is faster, runs without a browser, avoids token waste on flex/grid layout, and has a built-in agentic verification loop for audio, collisions and motion. He pushed past the last 10% of detail and is open-sourcing the template. The thread's best tension is exactly that last 10% - the original creator's point is that taste is the hard part, and a reply pushes back that Kovalenko's transitions are actually better. People also want to know which model (Astra) and whether Codex needed docs for a niche framework.
summary: A concrete example of code-native video beating a general-purpose editor on iteration speed, with the taste question still unresolved.

title: ObsidianUI ships an open-source dashboard shell after a three-hour build
author: Athrix
essence: Athrix spent three hours building a dashboard component and released it as open source in ObsidianUI, with a live docs page at obsidianui.dev/docs/dashboard-shell and a GitHub repo. The pitch is aimed squarely at paid UI libraries - 'every paid ui lib will hate us' - and the component uses duotone icons and FactoryAI in the build. The thread is small but positive, with people asking about the icon pack and recording tool and one noting that three hours for a polished shell is a sweet spot. The repo is also being pushed toward 1,000 stars, so this is early-stage and worth watching rather than adopting blind.
summary: A free dashboard shell for fast internal tools; the three-hour build is impressive, but the library is young and lightly tested.

title: Phone-use plus OpenAI's Decisions API lets an agent choose its next action 10x faster
author: Abdulla Ababakre
essence: Abdulla Ababakre pairs phone-use, his agent that operates a phone, with OpenAI's new Decisions API, which lets an app choose the right model, tool or action in near real time. OpenAI says Decisions is up to 10x faster than GPT-6 Luna through the Responses API, and the combo is aimed at the step where a phone agent has to decide what to tap next without a full model round-trip. Phone-use currently runs on Ababakre's own device cloud, with a local version promised soon. The thread is tiny, but the one substantive question - whether it can drive a physical iPhone rather than a hosted device - points at the gap between a demo and a product.
summary: A promising latency fix for phone agents; the missing piece is local/physical-device support, which is still promised rather than shipped.

title: Capy's Guided Reviews turn a big PR into chapters with a before/after overview
author: luffy
essence: Capy added Guided Reviews: instead of dumping a big diff in file order, it opens with a before/after overview, groups files into chapters explained in plain language, and orders the core change first with database, tests and generated files last. It shipped in Capy 0.4.4 alongside marketplace plugins, custom models on your own key and desktop threads without a project. The demo is polished enough that the main reply thread is an accusation - this looks like Linear's guided diffs - and luffy answers that it was inspired by Linear but Capy had it in v1, lost it in v2 and is bringing it back with its own review agent. Either way, the interaction pattern is becoming table stakes for agent-era code review.
summary: A good default structure for reviewing agent-sized diffs - overview, chapters, core-first ordering - regardless of whether Capy or Linear ships it better.

title: Blogr maps a niche, writes and publishes articles, then watches the rankings
author: Serg
essence: Serg pitches blogr.ai as an AI writer that does the whole loop rather than dumping random posts: it maps your niche, writes the articles, publishes them and watches the rankings, with the first article free. The post got almost no distribution - one bookmark and 879 views - which makes it a useful counterexample to the idea that launch copy alone creates traction. The same thread also promotes bytemail 1.0, a native Swift email app for Mac that handles Gmail, iCloud, Outlook, Yahoo and IMAP in one window with no web wrapper and no server in the mail path, suggesting Serg is shipping multiple small products rather than focusing on one.
summary: A standard AI-SEO content loop with no proof yet; the launch's near-zero engagement is the more informative signal.

title: Google's The Big Code competition is open to 2027-2029 grads, not 2026
author: TryingToFindAGoodUsername
essence: A quick signal boost for The Big Code, a Google coding competition hosted on HackerEarth. The important detail is eligibility: it is open to 2027, 2028 and 2029 graduates, and the poster - a 2026 grad - spends the thread complaining that his batch is excluded. Replies confirm the same frustration and ask whether this replaces Google Hash Code or Code Jam, which Google discontinued. For anyone in the eligible batches, the value is the direct HackerEarth link; for everyone else, it is a reminder to check graduation-year filters before investing time in a contest.
summary: Worth a look only if you graduate in 2027-2029; the thread is more useful for the eligibility warning than the competition itself.

title: The Burgery In, Indiranagar: buff and chicken burgers worth the trip
author: In her sandwich-making era
essence: A straight-up Bangalore burger recommendation: The Burgery In in Indiranagar does buff and chicken burgers, really crispy fries and a peanut butter shake that the poster calls soooo flavorful. In the thread she narrows it to the Ultimate and Frizzled burgers - the Frizzled has a melted crunchy layer of cheese - and says she liked it better than Truffles. Replies are the useful part: one compares it with Smash Guys (good burger, excellent bone-marrow side), another recommends Guerrilla Diner, and a third went for a birthday dinner and called it the best burger of their life. It is a low-stakes bookmark, but a well-validated one.
summary: A concrete Indiranagar burger pick with enough reply confirmation to trust; go for the Frizzled and the peanut butter shake.
